Emergency thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke: current evidence, international guidelines, and local clinical practice

Anderson CO Tsang, MB, BS, MRCSEd1; Ryo WL Yeung2; Mona MY Tse, MB, BS, FHKAM (Medicine)3; Raymand Lee, MB, BS, FHKAM (Radiology)4; WM Lui, MB, BS, FCSHK1

1 Division of Neurosurgery, Department of Surgery, Queen Mary Hospital, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam, Hong Kong

2 Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam, Hong Kong

3 Division of Neurology, Department of Medicine, Queen Mary Hospital, Pokfulam, Hong Kong

4 Department of Radiology, Queen Mary Hospital, Pokfulam, Hong Kong

Corresponding author: Dr Anderson CO Tsang ([[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection#ea8b89859e998b848daa82819fc48281))

[Full paper in PDF](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296.pdf)

Abstract

Acute ischaemic stroke due to large vessel occlusion leads to grave neurological morbidity and mortality. Conventional intravenous thrombolysis is ineffective in achieving timely reperfusion in this group of patients. The publication of five positive randomised controlled trials of emergency thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke in 2015 provided strong evidence to support endovascular reperfusion therapy and represented a paradigm shift in acute stroke management. In this article, we review the current evidence and international guidelines, and report on the findings of a survey study of the clinical practice and opinions of local neurologists, neurosurgeons, and interventional radiologists in emergency thrombectomy. We also discuss the controversies around thrombectomy treatment, local experience, and suggestions to incorporate thrombectomy in acute stroke treatment.

[[Abstract in Chinese]](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-chi.jpg)

Introduction

Before 2015, the standard of care for emergency ischaemic stroke treatment was intravenous thrombolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (IV-tPA). This stemmed from the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke trial in 1995, which showed that compared with placebo, patients who were given IV-tPA within 3 hours from symptom onset were 30% more likely to have minimal or no disability at 3 months.[1](#r1) The therapeutic window was further extended to 4.5 hours from symptom onset by the European Cooperative Acute Stroke Study III, which demonstrated similar benefits when IV-tPA was administered between 3 and 4.5 hours to selected patients.[2](#r2)

Nonetheless, in patients with ischaemia due to occlusion of a major cerebral artery, such as the intracranial internal carotid artery or the first and second segment of middle cerebral artery (M1, M2), the efficacy of intravenous thrombolysis was limited, with a recanalisation rate of only 4% to 30%.[3](#r3) This group of patients frequently had a grave neurological prognosis and high mortality owing to the large infarct territory, and could develop malignant cerebral oedema that required decompressive craniectomy.[4](#r4)

To improve the recanalisation rate, endovascular mechanical thrombectomy to remove the occluding clot was proposed. Early studies of this technique showed conflicting results and were attributed to poor patient selection and suboptimal endovascular devices that resulted in a low recanalisation rate, thus failing to show the expected benefits of endovascular thrombectomy.[5](#r5) [6](#r6) [7](#r7)

With modern improved thrombectomy devices, the publication of five positive randomised trials of acute mechanical thrombectomy for ischaemic stroke resulting from anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2015 marked a paradigm shift in stroke treatment.[8](#r8) [9](#r9) [10](#r10) [11](#r11) [12](#r12) Since then, emergency endovascular thrombectomy has been internationally regarded as the new standard of care for acute ischaemic stroke caused by major vessel occlusion, and is recommended by all major stroke guidelines.

Summary of current evidence

The five independent randomised controlled trials that provided strong evidence to support endovascular thrombectomy were MR CLEAN,[8](#r8) REVASCAT,[9](#r9) ESCAPE,[10](#r10) EXTEND-IA,[11](#r11) and SWIFT PRIME,[12](#r12) conducted in the US, Europe, and Australia from 2010 to 2015. Although there were differences in terms of inclusion and exclusion criteria, all five studies recruited only acute stroke patients with angiogram-proven major vessel occlusion in the anterior circulation, and used newer-generation thrombectomy devices (mostly stent retrievers) that achieved higher recanalisation rates than earlier devices used in previous trials.

All patients in the five trials were given IV-tPA as standard treatment when eligible, and were then randomised to receive endovascular thrombectomy or standard care alone. All these trials unanimously showed significant benefit in the thrombectomy group in terms of improved functional outcome at 3 months, as measured by the modified Rankin scale (mRS) [[Table 1](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-table-1.jpg)[8](#r8) [9](#r9) [10](#r10) [11](#r11) [12](#r12) [13](#r13)].

**Table 1.** Summary of functional outcome and mortality at 90 days of five thrombectomy for ischaemic stroke trials[8](#r8) [9](#r9) [10](#r10) [11](#r11) [12](#r12) [13](#r13)

Functional outcome benefit

A meta-analysis of the above five trials with a total of 1287 eligible patients showed that 46% of patients treated by endovascular thrombectomy achieved functional independence (mRS score, 0-2) at 90 days, compared with 26.5% of patients in the control group[13](#r13) ([Table 1](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-table-1.jpg)). The number needed-to-treat was 2.6 for one patient to improve functionally by at least 1 point on mRS. In terms of safety, there was no significant difference between the intervention group and the control group in symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (4.4% vs 4.3%; P=0.81) or mortality rate at 90 days (15.3% vs 18.9%; P=0.15).[13](#r13)

Moreover, the clinical benefit was maintained whether the patient was eligible to receive IV-tPA in the first place, and across all age-groups including the patients older than 80 years. Patients improved after thrombectomy regardless of the initial severity of stroke, as documented by the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and the initial Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score.

Therapeutic time frame

Regarding the treatment time frame, thrombectomy within 6 hours from symptom onset was consistently beneficial across all five thrombectomy trials. In the REVASCAT trial that included patients within 8 hours of symptom onset, the median onset-to-reperfusion time was still within 6 hours in the thrombectomy group, although no separate data were provided for those who presented between 6 and 8 hours.[9](#r9) Similarly, in the ESCAPE trial, which included patients up to 12 hours from stroke onset, the median time to reperfusion was 4 hours from symptom onset and very few patients beyond 6 hours were recruited.[10](#r10) At present, two clinical trials are underway to investigate the benefits of endovascular thrombectomy for anterior circulation stroke beyond 6 hours, and both require computed tomography (CT) perfusion or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to assess infarct core and perfusion mismatch to determine eligibility (NCT02586415, NCT02142283). Therefore, the efficacy and risk of anterior circulation thrombectomy beyond 6 hours without advanced imaging selection criteria are uncertain, and should be performed with discretion or in a clinical research setting.

Posterior circulation and the paediatric population

At present, there is no evidence from randomised trials regarding thrombectomy for posterior circulation large-vessel occlusion or paediatric patients.

Contemporary thrombectomy devices

One major improvement of these five trials[8](#r8) [9](#r9) [10](#r10) [11](#r11) [12](#r12) compared with previous negative thrombectomy trials[5](#r5) [6](#r6) [7](#r7) was the exclusive use of newer stent retriever devices and a consequent higher recanalisation rate. Near-complete/complete (TICI 2b/3) recanalisation was achieved in 59% to 88% of patients, compared with only 25% to 41% in early studies that used intra-arterial tPA and first-generation devices.[14](#r14)

Another contemporary thrombectomy device was the direct aspiration catheter (ADAPT technique),[15](#r15) which applied suction to remove the clot via a large-bore endovascular catheter ([Fig 1](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-fig-1.jpg)). This technique was supported by multiple single-centre series that showed comparable and sometimes superior results over stent retrievers, although none of these were head-to-head comparative trials.[16](#r16) [17](#r17) [18](#r18) The 2016 THERAPY trial was the only randomised study to compare aspiration thrombectomy versus IV-tPA alone.[19](#r19) It was terminated prematurely with a limited sample size after publication of the positive stent retriever trials, and as such failed to demonstrate a statistically significant benefit for aspiration thrombectomy over intravenous thrombolysis alone.

**Figure 1.** (a) Angiogram showing acute occlusion of the right middle cerebral artery (arrow). (b) Post-thrombectomy angiogram showing revascularisation of the right middle cerebral artery territory. (c) Thrombus removed by endovascular thrombectomy

Cost-effectiveness of thrombectomy

Cost-utility analyses have been performed in several health care systems around the world and all have shown the cost-effectiveness of endovascular thrombectomy. The cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained for thrombectomy over standard thrombolysis treatment varies between US$7988 (Sweden), US$9386 (US), US$11 651 (UK), and US$11 990 (Canada).[18](#r18) [20](#r20) [21](#r21) [22](#r22) Using internationally accepted willingness-to-pay per QALY threshold of the gross domestic product per capita, all of the above health care systems found endovascular thrombectomy to be cost-effective.

International guidelines

The overwhelming clinical evidence to support application of thrombectomy in anterior circulation stroke prompted the European Stroke Organisation (ESO) and subsequently the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association (AHA/ASA) to release a focused update of early stroke treatment guidelines in 2015, recommending endovascular thrombectomy with stent retriever device if onset of symptoms was within 6 hours and was due to a major vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation, and when suitable criteria were met (Class I, Level of Evidence A).[23](#r23) [24](#r24) The [Box](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj76294-box.jpg) lists the latest AHA/ASA and ESO recommendations regarding endovascular thrombectomy.[23](#r23) [24](#r24)

**Box.** New international guidelines for endovascular thrombectomy[23](#r23) [24](#r24)

Emergency thrombectomy in Hong Kong

Endovascular thrombectomy for ischaemic stroke is a relatively new procedure in Hong Kong and is not routinely available. Although it was practised in certain centres prior to 2015 for selected cases,[25](#r25) there was no consensus on treatment indications, patient selection criteria, or operative techniques. With acute mechanical thrombectomy now becoming the international standard of care for acute anterior circulation ischaemic stroke, we undertook a survey to identify the availability, clinical practice, and potential obstacles of an acute stroke thrombectomy service in Hong Kong.

Design of the survey

We designed a survey which addressed the availability of expertise, the indications, patient selection for stroke treatment, interventional techniques, and perceived obstacles to timely stroke treatment. This was a web-based survey consisting of 43 questions and was administered from May to August 2016. Respondents were drawn from the Hong Kong Stroke Society, Hong Kong Neurosurgical Society, and Hong Kong Society of Interventional and Therapeutic Neuroradiology. Invitations to participate were sent by email. Participants did not receive any incentive to complete this survey. We received 44 responses from the three societies. Background characteristics of the respondents are shown in [Figure 2](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-fig-2.jpg).

**Figure 2.** Background characteristics of respondents (n=44)

Service availability

Overall, 24 (54.5%) respondents from six public hospitals and five private practices were regularly involved in the decision and provision of mechanical thrombectomy for patients with acute ischaemic stroke. Most were neurosurgeons (75.0%), and the remainder were neurologists and interventional radiologists. In most centres, the interventionist capable of performing thrombectomy was a neurosurgeon or interventional radiologist, whereas in half of the responding centres there were also neurologists who were able to perform this procedure. For the majority of interventionists (62.5%), mechanical thrombectomy was offered only on an ‘ad hoc’ basis with no official service hours. The mean number of interventionists currently available was 4.3 per centre. The questions and responses of the survey are shown in [Table 2](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-table-2.jpg).

**Table 2.** Questions and responses on endovascular thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke (n=24)

Clinical practice

Direct aspiration technique (ADAPT[15](#r15)) was the most popular first-line thrombectomy technique, adopted by 83.3% of respondents. A stent retriever was chosen as a second-line thrombectomy device by 91.7% of interventionists. The majority of local practitioners used 6 hours as the time limit for anterior circulation thrombectomy in accordance with current guidelines, but a significant number of respondents (37.5%) adopted a more liberal limit of 8 hours or beyond. Most practitioners would prescribe intravenous thrombolysis using the standard dosage in patients who fulfilled thrombolysis indications, regardless of thrombectomy decision, and in line with current guidelines.

For patient selection, most local interventionists used CT angiography as the predominant imaging modality. This finding is unsurprising considering CT perfusion and MRI scanners were not routinely available in an emergency setting in many public hospitals where most acute stroke patients were treated. Apart from angiographic evidence of major vessel occlusion (intracranial internal carotid artery, M1/M2 segment of middle cerebral artery and basilar artery), stroke symptom severity of NIHSS score of >5 and pre-stroke functional status (mRS score ≤2) were regarded as important selection criteria by over 70% of respondents.

Up to 87.5% of respondents performed thrombectomy without general anaesthesia. This practice has been recommended after a recent meta-analysis that confirmed better outcome in patients treated under conscious sedation than in those under general anaesthesia.[26](#r26) A more recent randomised trial, however, showed no difference in outcome whether general anaesthesia or conscious sedation was used.[27](#r27)

Incorporating emergency thrombectomy in acute stroke care in Hong Kong

Locally, an acute ischaemic stroke service is heavily dependent on a public health system that handles over 80% of emergency hospital admissions in Hong Kong.[28](#r28) Our neurologists and stroke physicians in public hospitals have made major contributions over the past two decades in implementing intravenous thrombolysis and spearheading 24-hour acute stroke care. As a result of much effort, currently seven of 17 emergency hospitals in the public hospital system provide 24-hour IV-tPA thrombolysis service.[29](#r29) Future enhancement of an acute stroke service should aim to provide timely and universal access for patients with acute ischaemic stroke, and divert potentially eligible thrombectomy patients to centres that can provide such service ([Fig 3](https://www.hkmj.org/system/files/hkmj176296-fig-3.jpg)).

**Figure 3.** Treatment algorithm for patients with acute ischaemic stroke

Our survey identified the most common reported obstacles in implementing prompt stroke interventions as poor inter- and in-hospital logistics of patient transfer and triage, delayed presentation, and insufficient interventionists, as well as difficulty in obtaining emergency CT angiogram in an urgent setting.

The two-tier primary and comprehensive stroke centre model that aims to give priority access to patients with suspected acute stroke may be seen as a framework for acute stroke service.[30](#r30) [31](#r31) [32](#r32) The first-tier stroke centre should be capable of providing 24-hour urgent CT and CT angiogram with round-the-clock IV-tPA service. All patients with suspicious stroke symptoms, such as acute hemiplegia or dysphasia, should be directly transferred to one of these first-tier stroke centres, bypassing other non-stroke centres in emergency hospitals to avoid unnecessary delay in diagnosis. When major vessel occlusion is suspected, immediate CT angiography should be performed in the same setting to determine thrombectomy eligibility. Second-tier stroke centres should additionally be capable of 24-hour endovascular thrombectomy, and be equipped with full-time neurosurgery, neurocritical care, and advanced radiological imaging support.[31](#r31) Among the local stroke specialists, a median number of four second-tier comprehensive stroke centres is believed to be appropriate in Hong Kong. Support from the health administration, structured training for endovascular techniques, and efficient use of existing resources are required to effectively incorporate emergency thrombectomy into routine clinical service locally.

Conclusion

There is a strong body of clinical evidence and international guidelines to support emergency endovascular thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke due to anterior circulation major vessel occlusion. As the local stroke community embraces this new treatment modality, efforts should be directed towards providing universal and timely access to emergency ischaemic stroke therapy for the Hong Kong population.

Declaration

All authors have disclosed no conflicts of interest.

We thank Dr GKK Leung for his valuable advice in the course of this study. We also thank the Hong Kong Stroke Society, Hong Kong Neurosurgical Society, and Hong Kong Society of Interventional and Therapeutic Neuroradiology for their support in the survey study.

results.content:
Across the series, experts review expanded indications for thrombolysis and thrombectomy, updated neuroimaging paradigms, system-level readiness, and—for the first time—guideline recommendations for the acute management of pediatric ischemic stroke. Each video focuses on practical implications for clinical decision-making and institutional preparedness across diverse care settings.

# 2026 Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline Series: New Guidance for Healthcare Professionals

Acute ischemic stroke care continues to evolve rapidly, with new evidence reshaping prehospital triage, imaging, reperfusion strategies, and team-based care across the lifespan. This four-part video series features authors of the 2026 American Heart Association Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline highlighting practice-changing updates for emergency medicine clinicians, neurointerventionalists, imaging specialists, nurses, stroke coordinators, and pediatric stroke teams.

Across the series, experts review expanded indications for thrombolysis and thrombectomy, updated neuroimaging paradigms, system-level readiness, and—for the first time—guideline recommendations for the acute management of pediatric ischemic stroke. Each video focuses on practical implications for clinical decision-making and institutional preparedness across diverse care settings.

## Abstract

Please see the [Editorial Comment](https://www.ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28814) by Shalini A. Amukotuwa, discussing this article.

Endovascular thrombectomy has become the standard-of-care treatment for carefully selected patients with acute ischemic stroke due to a large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation. Neuroimaging plays a vital role in determining patient eligibility for thrombectomy, both in the early (0–6 hours from symptom onset) and late (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) time windows. Various neuroimaging algorithms are used to determine thrombectomy eligibility, and each algorithm must be optimized for institutional workflow. In this review, we describe common imaging modalities and recommended algorithms for the evaluation of patients for endovascular thrombectomy. We also discuss emerging patient populations who might qualify for thrombectomy in the coming years.

## HIGHLIGHTS

▪ _Neuroimaging for patient selection for thrombectomy should include exclusion of intracranial hemorrhage and identification of large-vessel occlusion in both late and early time windows._

▪ _The extent of ischemic injury can be assessed by perfusion imaging, which allows identification of the ischemic core and salvageable penumbra._

▪ _Neuroimaging protocols for patient selection for thrombectomy must be optimized to meet institutional workflows and available equipment._

Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) has a current global incidence of 7.59 million cases [[1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R1)]. The emergence of endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), performed using either a stentriever or an aspiration catheter, revolutionized the care of patients with AIS with large-vessel occlusion (AIS-LVO) of the anterior circulation (i.e., of the internal carotid artery [ICA], the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery [MCA], or the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery [ACA]), and EVT is currently the standard-of-care treatment for appropriate candidates [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. Landmark trials that showed the efficacy of EVT represented a distinct departure from the historic treatment of patients with AIS [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. These studies incorporated the use of neuroimaging, most notably to confirm a large-vessel occlusion (LVO), to determine patient eligibility for EVT in both early (0–6 hours from symptom onset) and late (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) time windows [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

Patients with AIS-LVO who are most likely to benefit from EVT have three characteristics on baseline neuroimaging: an LVO that is amenable to EVT; a small ischemic core (defined as the brain tissue considered to be likely infarcted); and critically hypoperfused brain tissue that, on the basis of the presence of an imaging or clinical mismatch, appears salvageable if recanalization of the occluded cervical or cerebral artery is achieved ([Fig. 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F1A)). Patients with a cerebral hemorrhage at baseline typically are also excluded from treatment [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. Assessment for EVT in patients with AIS-LVO may use a variety of CT and MRI techniques and protocols; these should be optimized for each hospital's workflow to expedite patient treatment.

Fig. 1A —43-year-old man with acute left middle cerebral artery (MCA) syndrome (NIH Stroke Scale score, 17). Patient initially underwent head CT performed at outside facility.

**A,** CT perfusion imaging (CTP) of cerebral blood flow (CBF) shows no ischemic core within left MCA territory.

**B,** CTP of time to maximum of tissue residue function (Tmax) shows penumbra of 78 mL.

Open in Viewer![Image 4](https://ajronline.org/cms/10.2214/AJR.22.28608/asset/images/large/22_28608_01c.jpeg)

Fig. 1C —43-year-old man with acute left middle cerebral artery (MCA) syndrome (NIH Stroke Scale score, 17). Patient initially underwent head CT performed at outside facility.

**C,** Maximum-intensity-projection (MIP) image from CTA confirms presence of left M1 segment occlusion (_arrow_). Patient was transferred to comprehensive stroke center and underwent brain MRI.

Fig. 1D —43-year-old man with acute left middle cerebral artery (MCA) syndrome (NIH Stroke Scale score, 17). Patient initially underwent head CT performed at outside facility.

In this review, we describe common imaging modalities and recommended algorithms for the selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT. We also discuss emerging areas of expanded treatment by EVT that are likely to alter clinical practice in the next several years.

## Noninvasive Imaging Techniques

### _Detection of Large-Vessel Occlusion_

Accurate identification of an LVO is crucial to determine EVT eligibility. Prior studies that failed to find a benefit of EVT did not include CTA or MRA as part of the enrollment criteria, and a large percentage of patients who were evaluated lacked evidence of an LVO by digital subtraction angiography performed before EVT was attempted [[11](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R11)–[13](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R13)]. More recent successful EVT trials included identification of an LVO by CTA or MRA as part of the enrollment criteria [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

The most commonly performed study to identify the presence of an LVO is CTA [[14](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R14)–[16](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R16)]. Most centers perform CTA by acquiring a single-phase acquisition, which is sufficient to evaluate cerebral arterial vasculature. Multiphase CTA, which was used as part of patient selection in the ESCAPE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01778335) trial, is less commonly performed and acquires images in the peak arterial, venous, and late venous phases [[17](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R17)]. Multiphase CTA has shown potential in helping to differentiate proximal ICA occlusion from pseudoocclusion (i.e., a column of stagnate nonopacified blood proximal to a true intracranial occlusion or severe stenosis that results in the appearance of an ICA occlusion) [[18](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R18)].

In patients who undergo MRI rather than CT before EVT, MRA is used to identify the presence of an LVO. Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA is the most common technique. On the TOF sequence, static tissue signal is nulled by repeated radiofrequency pulses, whereas inflowing blood remains unsaturated and hyper-intense due to continued movement [[19](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R19)]. Although TOF MRA provides diagnostic information similar to that of CTA for the detection of LVOs, the method is limited by lack of coverage of neck and medium-to-distal intracranial vessels. Alternatively, contrast-enhanced MRA includes the neck vessels but would result in two separate doses of gadolinium-based contrast material in patients who later undergo perfusion MRI. There is a lack of strong evidence that vascular imaging of the neck influences thrombectomy treatment decisions, procedural times, or procedural success.

CT perfusion imaging (CTP) or perfusion MRI has shown the potential to identify the presence of an LVO in patients who do not undergo CTA or MRA. In a study of patients with AIS, the combination of perfusion MRI and DWI alone resulted in 95.9% sensitivity and 98.4% specificity for the correct triage of EVT as well as for highly accurate localization to the ICA M1 (96%) or M2 (90%) segment [[20](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R20)]. CTP has also shown potential in helping to identify occlusions in more distal small and medium vessels [[21](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R21), [22](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R22)]. These results require prospective validation, and CTA or MRA remain the standard of care for LVO detection. Nonetheless, neurointerventionalists and neurologists routinely apply CTP or perfusion MRI using mobile software platforms to identify patients with an LVO who may benefit from EVT treatment.

### _Ischemic Core Delineation_

_Qualitative assessment of ischemia on noncontrast CT—_ Noncontrast CT remains the most common first-line imaging modality for AIS evaluation due to its widespread availability and the speed of imaging. However, detection of ischemia with noncontrast CT remains challenging, with a reported sensitivity of 26–48% [[23](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R23), [24](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R24)]. Early signs of ischemia on noncontrast CT include loss of differentiation between gray matter and white matter, sulcal effacement, and hypoattenuation of the basal ganglia, caudate head, and insula [[25](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R25)–[27](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R27)]. When correctly detected, these signs of ischemia can be qualitatively applied to measure the degree of ischemic injury. However, noncontrast CT is not useful for accurate volumetric segmentation of the ischemic core, as is made possible by CTP or other advanced CT techniques or by diffusion-weighted MRI techniques. Brain tissue that shows hypoattenuation on noncontrast CT is highly likely to be irreversibly infarcted, and recovery of hypoattenuating brain tissue in patients with AIS-LVO is rare [[28](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R28)].

_Semiquantitative ischemic core assessment using the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score—_ The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS) was developed as a method to standardize the assessment of ischemic injury on noncontrast CT [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29)]. ASPECTS divides the MCA territory into 10 separate regions and allocates 1 point per region. Points are removed when hypoattenuation is present within 50% or more of a region on noncontrast CT ([Fig. 2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F2A)). Currently, patients with LVO and an ASPECTS of 6 or greater are considered favorable candidates for EVT [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29)]. ASPECTS has proven to be effective for patient selection, as described later in this review, but the technique has poor interreader agreement [[29](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R29), [30](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R30)].

Although ASPECTS was a component of the imaging inclusion criteria in trials of thrombectomy at early time windows, it has not been used as part of imaging inclusion criteria in patients with AIS-LVO who present in the late time window (> 6 to 24 hours from symptom onset) [[5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5), [6](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R6)]. The DEFUSE 3 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02586415) trial excluded from treatment those patients who had an ASPECTS of less than 6. Therefore, selection of patients for EVT when they present more than 6 hours after symptom onset still relies on CTP or MRI to determine the volume of the ischemic core. A post hoc analysis of the DEFUSE 3 trial, which included patients who were screened but not enrolled in the study, found that patients in the late time window who had an ASPECTS of 8–10 had small ischemic core volumes, whereas patients with an ASPECTS of 5–7 had highly variable ischemic core volumes [[31](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R31)]. These findings suggest that some patients with lower ASPECTS may not be favorable EVT candidates.

_Quantitative volumetric ischemic core assessment using CT perfusion imaging and DWI—_ DWI is an accurate and widely accepted technique for establishing ischemic core volume. DWI sequences are highly sensitive to the diffusion of water molecules in tissues. With the development of tissue ischemia, dysfunction of the sodium-potassium cell membrane pump due to loss of cellular energy results in restriction of water molecules and cellular swelling [[32](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R32)]. These changes correspond to hyperintense tissue on DWI and hypointense tissue on the ADC map [[33](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R33), [34](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R34)]. An ADC of less than 620 × 10−6 mm 2/s is considered the optimal threshold for delineation of the ischemic core [[35](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R35)]. Although increased signal on DWI at the recommended ADC threshold is clinically characterized as irreversibly infarcted tissue, this signal can be partially reversed, especially in early time windows; thus, the concept of the ischemic core is controversial [[36](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R36)].

Although DWI is a highly accurate method for delineating the ischemic core, MRI is less widely available, especially in the emergency department setting. Therefore, CT techniques that are capable of ischemic core identification and delineation have been developed over the years. CTP is the most commonly used technique for estimation of the ischemic core in patients with AISLVO. The ischemic core is commonly measured as a reduction in cerebral blood flow (CBF) of more than 70% or a significant reduction of cerebral blood volume (CBV) in the hemisphere affected by the stroke compared with the contralateral hemisphere [[37](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R37)]. Reduced CBF and CBV thresholds that best estimate the ischemic core vary by software platform, and commercial software is often purposely designed to underestimate the ischemic core volume to reduce the risk of inadvertent exclusion from EVT treatment [[37](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R37)]. Patients with AIS-LVO and an ischemic core volume of 50–70 mL or less are considered favorable candidates for EVT treatment [[7](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R7)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. Whether patients with larger ischemic core volumes also benefit from thrombectomy remains uncertain, and ongoing trials are testing whether these patients benefit from EVT.

Although CTP estimation of the ischemic core is accurate in most patients, CTP interpretation has numerous potential pitfalls [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)]. The potential for overestimation of the ischemic core in patients presenting within the first 60–90 minutes after they were last known to be well and for underestimation of the ischemic core due to delayed collateral recruitment warrant particular attention, with noncontrast CT findings considered [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)]. Given the potential variability of CTP results, the interpretation should be integrated with consideration of the patient's clinical status.

### _Penumbra Evaluation_

The penumbra represents the hypoperfused brain tissue that surrounds the ischemic core. The penumbra is salvageable if the occluded artery that is causing the stroke is recanalized to restore blood flow to the brain [[39](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R39)]. Therefore, salvage of the penumbra and assessment for a volume mismatch between the ischemic core and penumbra are at the foundation of selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT.

Quantification of the penumbra is possible by CTP, perfusion MRI, or other advanced MRI techniques such as arterial spin labeling. These imaging techniques produce quantitative and visual assessments of the penumbra that can be applied quickly and easily to assess patient eligibility for EVT treatment. Commercialized automated systems quantify perfusion data and present the ischemic core and penumbral volumes, allowing treating physicians to quickly determine whether the penumbra is sufficiently larger than the ischemic core to justify treatment ([Fig. 3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F3)). Typically, the volume of the penumbra should be at least 15 mL greater than the volume of the ischemic core, and the ratio of the penumbra volume to the ischemic core volume should be at least 1.2–1.8 [[40](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R40)].

The use of perfusion imaging to identify and quantify the penumbra is not universally adopted, and critics of the technique argue that perfusion imaging is not necessary and may exclude from EVT those patients who may benefit from such intervention. By contrast, the FRAME (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03875820) study provides evidence that the identification of the penumbra and of patients with a mismatch between core and penumbra, even in early time windows, may help to identify patients who are likely to benefit from EVT [[41](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R41)]. This prospective study acquired perfusion imaging before EVT in patients with AIS-LVO who were 0–6 hours from symptom onset. However, perfusion imaging was not processed or evaluated by the treating physicians before EVT, such that treatment decisions were not determined by the presence of a mismatch profile. Once the perfusion imaging was processed, patients who had a perfusion match profile without evidence of a salvageable penumbra were found to have significantly lower rates of good outcomes compared with patients with evidence of a salvageable penumbra.

Multiple imaging techniques may be used to delineate the penumbra. These techniques are associated with variable parameter maps and thresholds, depending on the vendor of the software that is used to process the perfusion data. This topic is discussed at greater depth by Vagal et al. [[38](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R38)].

Although CTP and perfusion MRI are important techniques to aid in patient selection for EVT in the setting of AIS-LVO, alternative techniques such as arterial spin labeling could help illustrate the presence and relative size of penumbra. In addition, mismatch between the core and clinical symptoms, whereby the volume of core infarct underrepresents the patient's clinical symptoms, was part of the inclusion criteria for the DAWN (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02142283) trial, and can be used to determine EVT eligibility [[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)].

## Imaging Algorithms for Thrombectomy Candidate Identification

The MR CLEAN (Netherlands Trial Registry number NTR1804) trial and the THRACE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01062698) trial were the first randomized trials to show the efficacy of EVT for patients with AIS-LVO, with both trials requiring noncontrast CT to rule out intracranial hemorrhage and with CTA or MRA required to identify an LVO [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3), [4](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R4)]. The REVASCAT (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01692379) trial used a more refined imaging algorithm for patient selection that included ASPECTS (ASPECTS of > 6 on noncontrast CT or > 5 on DWI) as well as CTA or MRA [[5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5)]. REVASCAT found that EVT plus medical therapy led to higher rates of favorable outcomes compared with medical therapy alone in patients who presented within 8 hours from symptom onset, with a stronger treatment effect compared with the MR CLEAN trial [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3), [5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R5)].

The ESCAPE trial extended the treatment window for EVT to up to 12 hours from symptom onset by including patients with ASPECTS of 6 or greater and favorable arterial collaterals on CTA [[6](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R6)]. Patients were defined as having good-to-moderate collaterals on single-phase or multiphase CTA when filling of 50% or more of the MCA pial arterial circulation was shown, as compared with the normal contralateral side ([Fig. 4](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F4A)).

The EXTEND-IA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01492725) and SWIFT PRIME (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01657461) studies incorporated the use of perfusion imaging for selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT up to 6 hours from symptom onset [[7](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R7), [8](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R8)]. The DEFUSE 3 and DAWN trials showed that EVT was superior to medical therapy alone for the treatment of AIS-LVO in eligible patients who were last known to be well from 6 to either 16 or 24 hours after symptom onset [[9](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R9), [10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. Both studies used perfusion imaging or DWI to quantify the ischemic core volumetrically. The DEFUSE 3 trial used the presence of mismatch by CTP or perfusion MRI to select patients for thrombectomy treatment. The DAWN trial inclusion criteria incorporated the presence of mismatch between the perfusion core and clinical symptoms. Details of the imaging criteria for these landmark trials are summarized in [Table 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#tab1).

## Recommended Imaging Algorithms

Many reasonable imaging protocols can accurately and expeditiously identify potential EVT candidates, and each center should implement a workflow that is optimized for the individual hospital environment [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2), [42](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R42)]. For example, a hospital that acts as a central referral hub may require a different imaging algorithm and work-flow than the referring hospitals that it serves. This section presents a nonexhaustive set of suggested imaging algorithms.

### _Early Time Window (0–6 Hours From Symptom Onset)_

Several imaging algorithms are accepted for patients with AIS-LVO who present in early time windows [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. This imaging must exclude intracranial hemorrhage, identify the presence of an LVO, and provide at least a qualitative assessment of the degree of ischemic injury before consideration of EVT. At a minimum, patients should undergo noncontrast CT and CTA to determine EVT eligibility. A more complex imaging protocol that includes the application of ASPECTS, multiphase CTA for improved arterial collateral assessment, or CTP for ischemic core and target mismatch quantification is reasonable and is often used at U.S. stroke centers. MRI-based techniques such as MRA, DWI, and perfusion MRI may be used in place of CT at centers with rapid MRI access.

### _Late Time Window (> 6 to 24 Hours From Symptom Onset)_

The evaluation of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT in late time windows requires advanced imaging based on current guidelines [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. In late time windows, brain imaging must exclude the presence of intracranial hemorrhage, identify the presence of an LVO, quantify the ischemic core volume, and identify a mismatch between the ischemic core volume and either the penumbra volume or the severity of the patient's clinical deficits. At a minimum, patients should undergo noncontrast CT, CTA, and CTP or comparable MRI-based techniques, so their eligibility for EVT can be determined. It is reasonable to apply the DEFUSE 3 ischemic core criteria (i.e., ischemic core volume < 70 mL) to patients who present within 16 hours of symptom onset [[43](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R43)]. This same threshold is likely reasonable to apply in patients who present within 24 hours of symptom onset. However, the ischemic core volume at this later time of presentation varies by age, and the DAWN criteria are likely more accurate ([Table 1](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#tab1)).

## Future Areas for Treatment Expansion

The success of stroke investigators in providing robust evidence that EVT is an effective therapy for AIS-LVO has revolutionized the treatment of eligible patients. However, much uncertainty remains as to whether other patients with AIS-LVO who fall outside the previously described clinical and imaging criteria may also benefit from EVT. Trials designed to expand treatment eligibility in patients with AIS-LVO are ongoing. In this section, we describe emerging areas of EVT treatment of ischemic stroke ([Fig. 5](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#F5)).

### _Patients With Mild Symptoms (NIH Stroke Scale < 6) and a Large-Vessel Occlusion_

The landmark EVT clinical trials required an NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 6 or greater, with some exceptions in the MR CLEAN and EXTEND-IA trials [[3](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R3)–[10](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R10)]. However, some patients with AIS-LVO present with mild symptoms, and it remains uncertain whether these patients should be treated by EVT acutely in an effort to improve long-term clinical outcomes. Data regarding EVT treatment decisions in patients with AIS-LVO and mild symptoms are mixed [[44](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R44)]. A meta-analysis of patients with an NIHSS score of 0–10 who were enrolled in early time window trials showed a nonsignificant difference supporting EVT, but the study cohort included patients with an NIHSS score of 6–10, thus meeting current EVT treatment criteria [[45](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R45)]. However, a retrospective study of patients with an NIHSS score of less than 6 found a lower rate of functional independence after EVT treatment [[46](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R46)].

The ENDOLOW (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01657461) and MOSTE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01657461) trials are ongoing randomized trials focused on EVT efficacy in patients with stroke who present with a low NIHSS score and an LVO of the proximal anterior circulation [[47](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R47), [48](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R48)]. Both studies are enrolling patients with an NIHSS score of less than 6 and an LVO of the intracranial ICA or M1 segment of the MCA territory. For both trials, the primary outcome measure is functional outcomes at 90 days.

### _Patients With Large Ischemic Cores_

Increased size of the ischemic core correlates with a greater likelihood of a poor clinical outcome after EVT [[49](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R49)]. However, whether patients with large ischemic cores still benefit from EVT compared with medical therapy is undetermined. A meta-analysis of the early time window trials found a benefit of EVT in patients who present with an ASPECTS of 3–5 but not in those with an ASPECTS of 0–2 [[45](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R45)]. The recent randomized RESCUE-Japan LIMIT (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03702413) trial provided the first high-level evidence of benefit with EVT for patients with an MRI ASPECTS of 3–5 [[50](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R50)]. The trial showed a significantly improved 90-day outcome for patients undergoing EVT plus standard medical care, although the rate of intracranial hemorrhage also significantly increased in patients who underwent EVT [[50](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R50)]. Additional randomized trials are needed to further determine the efficacy of EVT in patients with large ischemic cores, and several trials addressing this question are ongoing. Studies are also needed to assess for similar benefit when CT ASPECTS are applied. The TENSION (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03094715) trial will enroll patients with an ASPECTS of 3–5 within 12 hours of symptom onset [[51](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R51)]. The SELECT2 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03876457) trial will enroll patients with either an ASPECTS of 3–5 or a core infarct volume of 50 mL or greater within 24 hours of symptom onset [[52](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R52)]. The LASTE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03811769) trial will enroll patients with an ASPECTS of 5 or less within 7 hours of symptom onset [[53](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R53)]. The TESLA (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03805308) trial is enrolling patients with an ASPECTS of 2–5 within 24 hours of symptom onset [[54](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R54)]. The results of these randomized trials are highly anticipated and may result in further expansion of EVT treatment in this population.

### _Patients 90 Years Old or Older_

Current evidence supporting EVT was largely developed on the basis of findings for patients 18–89 years old and supports EVT as effective in eligible patients in this age range. The effectiveness of EVT for the treatment of patients older than 90 years is uncertain. Available retrospective data are mixed as to whether EVT is effective in these patients. In a small retrospective study of EVT that compared patients 80–89 years old and those 90–99 years old, those who were 90–99 years old had a significantly increased rate of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage and a nonsignificant increase in the 90-day mortality rate [[55](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R55)]. Another retrospective study that compared patients 90 years old or older to patients younger than 90 years old likewise showed increased rates of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage, although the two groups achieved similar rates of functional independence [[56](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R56)]. A meta-analysis of the feasibility, efficacy, and safety of EVT in patients older than 90 years old showed a high rate of futile revascularization [[57](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R57)]. The selection of older patients for EVT is likely to be heavily influenced by additional factors, such as baseline functional status and preexisting comorbidities. Although EVT treatment decisions require particular caution in patients 90 years old or older, neurointerventionalists will generally consider treatment in certain patients in this age range.

### _Patients With Medium-Vessel Occlusions_

As previously described, clear evidence indicates that patients with an anterior circulation LVO benefit from EVT. However, many patients present with vessel occlusions that are more distal than the M1 segment of the MCA, and whether EVT is an effective treatment in these patients remains uncertain. Currently, EVT of MCA occlusions of the M2 and M3 segments in carefully selected patients have a class IIB recommendation, in accordance with the guidelines of the American Heart Association and the American Stroke Association [[2](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R2)]. Although retrospective studies of EVT for medium-vessel occlusions use an NIHSS score threshold of 6 or greater for patient selection, these patients are more likely than those with an LVO to have mild stroke symptoms on presentation [[58](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R58)–[60](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R60)]. However, the presence of mild stroke symptoms on initial presentation does not necessarily result in better long-term functional outcomes [[61](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R61)]. Several randomized controlled trials are currently recruiting patients to assess the efficacy of thrombectomy for MVOs. However, new thrombolytics and neuroprotectants may further improve medical management, which may result in a lack of equipoise as a basis for further investigation of EVT treatment [[62](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R62)–[65](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R65)]. EVT of even more distal middle-vessel occlusions remains an area of interest that will require further high-level evidence of efficacy [[66](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R66)].

### _Patients With Posterior Circulation Large-Vessel Occlusion_

The previously described EVT trials included patients with anterior circulation LVOs. However, whether EVT benefits patients with vertebral or basilar artery occlusions was, until very recently, inconclusive. Two early randomized trials, Balanced Solution Versus Saline in Intensive Care Study (BASICS) and Bypass Surgery Versus Everolimus-Eluting Stent Implantation for Multivessel Coronary Artery Disease (BEST), found no significant difference between EVT and medical therapy alone for the treatment of basilar artery occlusion [[67](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R67), [68](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R68)]. A systemic review and meta-analysis from 2022 evaluated randomized trials and prospective cohort studies that compared technical success and functional outcomes between patients with anterior circulation LVO and posterior circulation LVO. Patients with posterior circulation LVO showed rates of recanalization comparable to those of patients with an anterior circulation LVO but also had a decreased rate of favorable functional outcomes [[69](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R69)]. The studies in this meta-analysis likely had overly broad inclusion criteria and thus failed to identify the population of patients with posterior circulation LVO who are likely to benefit from EVT.

Two trials published in 2022 provided the first prospective high-level evidence of benefit with EVT compared with medical therapy for the treatment of basilar artery occlusion. The ATTENTION (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04751708) trial recruited patients with basilar artery occlusion up to 12 hours after symptom onset and were assigned to EVT or best medical management in a 2:1 ratio [[70](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R70)]. A total of 46% of patients in the EVT arm achieved better functional outcomes (modified Rankin Scale [mRS] at 90 days, 0 to 3) compared with 23% of patients who received best medical management alone (adjusted risk ratio, 2.06; 95% CI, 1.46–2.91). Similarly, the BAOCHE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02737189) trial recruited patients who presented within 6–24 hours after symptom onset [[71](https://ajronline.org/doi/10.2214/AJR.22.28608#core-collateral-R71)]. Results showed that 46% of patients in the EVT arm achieved the primary outcome (mRS at 90 days, 0–3) compared with 24% of patients who received best medical management alone (adjusted rate ratio, 1.81; 95% CI, 1.26–2.60).

## Conclusion

Neuroimaging is critical in the selection of patients with AIS-LVO for EVT treatment. Brain imaging should verify the absence of intracranial hemorrhage, verify the presence of an LVO, and provide at least a qualitative assessment of the ischemic core (in early time windows) or a quantitative assessment of the ischemic core (in late time windows). Additional use of clinical and perfusion imaging to identify the presence of a mismatch between the ischemic core and the salvageable penumbra is often used in early time windows and should always be performed in late time windows. Regardless of the imaging algorithm used for EVT selection, the algorithm should be optimized for institutional workflow and applied in a consistent manner.

results.title: Advances in mechanical thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke
results.content:
At present, level 1a evidence still supports the use of advanced imaging, MRI, or CT perfusion for the selection of patients in the extended time window. However, recent publication of the MR CLEAN-LATE trial and upcoming results from the RESILIENT-EXTEND trial might lead to further widening of these imaging selection criteria.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Abstract

Mechanical thrombectomy is a ground breaking treatment for acute ischaemic stroke caused by occlusion of a large vessel. Its efficacy over intravenous thrombolysis has been proven in multiple trials with a lower number needed to treat than percutaneous coronary intervention for acute myocardial infarction. However, access to this key treatment modality remains limited with a considerable postcode lottery across the UK and many parts of the world. The evidence base for mechanical thrombectomy dates back to 2015. Since then, there have been important advances in establishing and widening the criteria for treatment. This narrative review aims to summarise the current evidence base and latest advances for physicians and academics with an interest in recanalisation treatments for acute ischaemic stroke.

**Keywords:**stroke, interventional radiology, neurology

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Introduction

The treatment of acute ischaemic stroke was revolutionised in 2015 after the publication of several landmark randomised controlled trials.[1–7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R1) These trials compared best medical treatment with endovascular treatment and confirmed the benefit of mechanical thrombectomy in anterior circulation large vessel occlusion. The result was definitive, with a significant increase in the proportion of patients who were alive and independent at three months, and a number needed to treat of between three and seven. [Figure 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#F1) demonstrates the efficacy of mechanical thrombectomy (MT) when compared with other interventions.[1 3–13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R1) The HERMES (Highly Effective Reperfusion Evaluated in Multiple Endovascular Stroke) trials[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R7) led to the provision of rapid, arterial recanalisation in the form of endovascular treatment at comprehensive stroke centres for patients presenting with acute ischaemic stroke within 6 hours of symptom onset time. An estimated 10% of patients with stroke are eligible for mechanical thrombectomy, but in the UK approximately 3% of stroke patients are currently offered this treatment.[14 15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R14) Considering that the UK health service's Long Term Plan is to increase access to this vital stroke treatment, our aim is to describe the advances in mechanical thrombectomy and summarise the current evidence base to allow better patient selection and management of patients with acute ischaemic stroke.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R16)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Sources and selection criteria

Between September 2022 and November 2022, we conducted a search of all articles in English relating to mechanical thrombectomy for acute ischaemic stroke in the following databases: PubMed, Embase, OVID, and Google Scholar. There were no date restrictions. We searched alternative iterations of mechanical thrombectomy and stroke such as “endovascular therapy,” “intra-arterial clot retrieval,” “endovascular thrombectomy,” “acute ischaemic stroke,” and “acute stroke.” Priority was given to peer reviewed systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and randomised controlled trials as well as existing clinical guidelines, because they had the most impact on changing clinical practice.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Big five trials on mechanical thrombectomy

Thrombectomy has been conducted for over two decades, but the evidence base proving efficacy and cost effectiveness was initially lacking. In the early 2010s, the first three randomised controlled trials looking at interventional procedures failed to show benefit of MT but had their limitations, including one trial (IMS-III), which did not require direct vascular imaging evidence of large vessel occlusion for the selection of patients.[17–19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R17) This trial was swiftly followed in 2015 with the publication of five randomised controlled trials comparing the efficacy of MT (using second generation thrombectomy devices) in addition to intravenous thrombolysis where eligible versus intravenous thrombolysis alone.[1 3–6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R1) All five trials focused on the anterior circulation exclusively, and four of the trials recruited patients in windows of up to 8 hours from symptom onset. Outcomes were measured using the modified Rankin score, which is an ordinal score from 0 to 6, with 0 meaning free of disability and six meaning death.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R20) MR CLEAN was the first positive trial to be published.[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R6) The results were compelling and prompted the data safety monitoring boards of the remaining trials to conduct interim analyses, leading to the early stoppage of these trials. The five trials ([table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#T1)) included over 1200 patients in total, and their data were combined in the HERMES meta-analysis.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R7) The researchers of this trial concluded that MT led to significantly better “good functional outcomes,” as defined by a modified Rankin score of 0-2. Patients treated with MT achieved the primary outcome in 46% of participants, compared with 26.5% receiving the best medical treatment (adjusted common odds ratio 2.49, 95% confidence interval 1.76 to 3.53, P<0.001). The number needed to treat to achieve a reduction in modified Rankin score of 1 point in one patient was 2.6. The pooled data allowed the meta-analysis to investigate the efficacy of thrombectomy across a variety of patient characteristics and showed that adult patients benefited from thrombectomy across all age groups and geographical locations. The benefit remained in patients who did not receive intravenous thrombolysis.

Strict time criteria were applied to the patients recruited in the HERMES collaboration.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R7) ESCAPE had the longest inclusion window of 12 hours from symptom onset.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R4) SWIFT-PRIME, MR CLEAN, and EXTEND-IA recruited patients up to 6 hours from symptom onset and REVASCAT up to 8 hours.[3 5 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R3) A subsequent meta-analysis demonstrated that most benefit was received from thrombectomy when conducted under 7 hours and 18 minutes.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R21) This reinforced the idea of the time clock; and similar to intravenous thrombolysis, an emphasis was placed on rapid recanalisation and reperfusion if good functional independence was to be achieved.

Following the results of the HERMES meta-analysis, best practice guidelines were updated in the USA, Canada, Europe, and the UK and mechanical thrombectomy became the preferred method for patients who have acute ischaemic stroke and presenting with an anterior circulation large vessel occlusion.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Procedural considerations of mechanical thrombectomy

MT is an endovascular procedure performed under fluoroscopic guidance and involves recanalisation of an intracranial occlusion by removing a thrombus using a retrievable stent (stent retriever), aspiration catheter, or a combination of both techniques. The procedure is typically performed via transfemoral arterial access but can be performed via the radial artery. A biaxial or triaxial catheter system is used, with progressively smaller calibre catheters sited within the distal vasculature. A large bore guide catheter is positioned proximally in the target great vessel, and digital subtraction angiography is acquired after injection of iodinated contrast confirming the large vessel occlusion.

Two main techniques for clot retrieval exist. A direct aspiration technique involves navigation of an aspiration catheter to the occlusion followed by syringe or pump driven aspiration.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R22) Alternatively, deployment of a stent retriever involves navigating a microwire and microcatheter beyond the occlusion. The stent retriever is unsheathed within the thrombus, allowing time for integration with the stent before being retrieved along with the thrombus. A combined stent retrieval aspiration technique can be used by additionally placing an aspiration catheter at the proximal margin of the thrombus.[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R23) The COMPASS study showed no significant difference between the two approaches with respect to both good functional outcome at 90 days (modified Rankin score 0-2, 52% (95% confidence interval 43.8% to 60.3%) in aspiration arm _v_ 50% (41.6% to 57.4%) in stent retrieval) and recanalisation rates. Aspiration approach had the added advantage of reduced costs and an 11 minute reduction in time to recanalisation (P=0.02).[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R24)

The second generation thrombectomy devices of the HERMES trials, including Solitaire (Medtronic) or Trevo (Stryker) stent retrievers, had improved successful reperfusion rates of 71% compared with first generation thrombectomy devices as defined by modified thrombolysis in cerebral infarction grades 2b or 3 ([figure 2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#F2)).[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R7)

When patients are selected for thrombectomy, practice varies between centres about performing the procedure under general anaesthesia or with conscious sedation. General anaesthesia confers the advantages of immobilisation to enable safe endovascular intervention with short delays in the induction of patients. By contrast, with conscious sedation, patients have faster times from door to groin puncture, but with the possibility of patient agitation complicating the procedure.[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R26) Initial meta-analysis data from the HERMES trials and three single centre, randomised controlled trials raised concern that general anaesthesia led to worse outcomes (adjusted common odds ratio 1.53, 95% confidence interval 1.14 to 2.04, P=0.004).[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R27) Recent meta-analysis from newer trials has suggested that, with a small effect size, patients treated under general anaesthesia achieve better functional outcomes (modified Rankin score 0-2, odds ratio 1.11, 95% confidence interval 1.03 to 1.2, P=0.007).[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R28) More work is needed to determine superiority. Patient factors should be considered when determining suitability for general anaesthesia.

Optimal management of peri-procedural blood pressure is important because within infarcted and penumbral tissue, cerebral autoregulation is impaired. In persistent large vessel occlusion, a retrospective analysis of 80 patients showed that blood pressure fluctuations and drops in blood pressure contributed to penumbral tissue loss.[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R29) In the case of hypertension, if patients receive intravenous thrombolysis, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommend that blood pressure should be less than 185 mm Hg (systolic) and 110 mm Hg (diastolic) to reduce the risk of haemorrhagic transformation.[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R30) The BP-TARGET randomised controlled trial including 324 patients failed to demonstrate a reduction in rates of radiological haemorrhagic transformation, with more intensive blood pressure lowering to 100-120 mm Hg systolic for the first 24-36 hours after thrombectomy.[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R31) In ENCHANTED2-MT, a multicentre, international, randomised controlled trial of 821 patients, researchers showed that intensive management of systolic blood pressure below 120 mm Hg led to worsening functional outcomes on the shift analysis for modified Rankin score at 90 days (odds ratio 1.37, 95% confidence interval 1.07 to 1.76, P=0.01).[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R32)

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Patient selection

After the adoption of MT globally, pathways have been developed to identify eligible patients with stroke who have large vessel occlusion. Patients either present to comprehensive stroke centres that are MT capable or to local primary stroke centres, which can refer to the nearest comprehensive stroke centre for definitive management. The key goal is rapid clinical and radiological assessment in tandem by stroke physicians and interventional neuroradiologists.

For physicians, the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is an 11-category rating scale developed to act as a framework for the identification and monitoring of neurological deficits seen with stroke syndromes.[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R33) Based on data from the HERMES trials, MT protocols select patients with at least moderate strokes with an NIHSS score ≥6.[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R34)

Once a patient has been determined to have a clinically significant clinical stroke syndrome, it is essential to clarify the pre-morbid level of independence. The HERMES trials excluded patients who were functionally dependent before their stroke. As such, in the UK, MT is often reserved for patients with a modified Rankin score between 0 and 2.

Subsequent brain and vascular imaging in the form of non-contrast computed tomography (CT) and CT angiography should be performed to identify a large vessel occlusion and the degree of established early ischaemic change. Class 1a evidence supports the use of MT in patients with a proximal large vessel occlusion involving the terminal internal carotid artery and/or the proximal M1 branch of the middle cerebral artery.[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R7) MR CLEAN, EXTEND-IA, and ESCAPE did additionally include patients with M2 occlusions. The degree of early ischaemic change is defined by the ASPECTS (Alberta Stroke Protocol Early CT Score, [figure 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#F4)). In the HERMES collaboration, patients with ASPECTS <6 were excluded because they had extensive early ischaemic change, suggesting less benefit to be gained from MT.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072)Mechanical thrombectomy for extended time windows (6-24 hours)

The HERMES collaboration clearly defined the importance of the time clock and showed that early intervention led to more favourable outcomes. Beyond 7 hours and 20 minutes after symptom onset, patients were less likely to achieve functional independence within three months.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R21) Only two of the five HERMES trials included any patients presenting in the late window (defined as 6-24 hours from symptom onset or last known being well (ie, when the patient was last known to be without the signs and symptoms of the current stroke or at their baseline)). Patients with unclear symptom onset or those with wake-up syndromes, representing up to 20% of presentations of acute ischaemic stroke, were excluded.[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R35)

When a large vessel occlusion occurs, deeper structures supplied by the vascular territory that lack collateral blood supply will infarct first. The areas of brain tissue with irreversible ischaemic damage are known as the ischaemic core. However, the part of the vascular territory surviving on collateral flow (ie, small vessels supplying ischaemic tissue through retrograde flow) is known as the ischaemic penumbra; this area of potentially salvageable brain tissue demonstrates reversible ischaemia if reperfusion is achieved. Patients can be phenotypically different and progress to complete infarction at different rates. In one study, 25% of patients termed as fast progressors lose 27 million neurons per minute, compared with 55% of patients termed as slow progressors who lose 35 000 neurons per minute. The quality of collateral flow was the predominant factor influencing infarct growth.[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R36)

Advanced neuroimaging techniques such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and CT perfusion can be used to evaluate the size of the ischaemic core and viable penumbra. The two landmark trials evaluating patients presenting in the late windows were the DAWN (n=206) and DEFUSE-3 (n=182) trials.[9 10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#R9) The DEFUSE-3 trial incorporated radiological mismatch between core and penumbra to define its inclusion criteria. Patients presenting 6-16 hours from last known being well, inclusive of wake-up syndromes, were included if they had a core infarct volume <70 mL and a mismatch ratio between the core and penumbra of ≥1.8 ([figure 6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414072#F6) shows an example). A different paradigm of a clinical radiological mismatch up to 24 hours was used in the DAWN trial. Patients had large clinical deficits but small ischaemic cores on advanced imaging. The clinical deficit, defined by NIHSS, was used as a surrogate marker for penumbra volume. Both trials showed that with the use of advanced imaging techniques, this carefully selected group of late presenters with a substantial core penumbra mismatch had improved functional neurological recovery. A limitation of these trials was inclusion of patients with unclear onset time or wake-up syndromes. Patients were included on the basis of their time last known well, but the true onset of stroke symptoms could have been shortly before waking. Fifty per cent of patients in DEFUSE-3 and 55% of patients in DAWN had a wake-up syndrome.
